text:
The premise is false, so don't use it. Einstein didn't fail math. He was strong at it from early on and had mastered calculus by about 15. At 16 he failed the entrance exam to ETH Zurich, but only because of the non-science sections (French, for example). His math and physics scores were excellent. Your kid can easily look this up, and then the lesson backfires: "even the myth was false, so what else are you telling me?"

"Grades don't matter" is also overstated. They affect course placement, scholarships, and admissions, and they often reflect habits (effort, consistency) that do matter. A more accurate and more durable message:

- Grades measure performance on specific tasks at a specific time. They don't measure intelligence, worth, or potential.
- A bad grade is information about what to fix, not a verdict.
- Learning and effort matter more than the number, though the number isn't irrelevant.

If you want a real example of someone whose early setbacks didn't define them, there are plenty. Einstein's ETH failure is true, but it was a narrow, fixable gap, which is itself a useful point: he retook a year of school and got in. Which age is your kid? The framing differs for a 7-year-old versus a 15-year-old.
